title: Théorie arithmétique. Théorie de Galois des motifs (1965) : notes manuscites (s.d.), tapuscrit (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This page has nothing to do with motives. It is page 46 of a typed course on analytic functions of several variables over K = R or C. It is probably a Grothendieck course text or a polycopié whose back was reused for the motif notes. The neighbouring pages are handwritten notes on Picard/Gr-categories, Dedekind-type categories and norms.

Content, in modern terms:
(1) Corollary (homotopy invariance of path integrals). Let ω = Σ f_k dx_k have holomorphic (or analytic) coefficients and satisfy the closedness conditions (1), presumably ∂f_j/∂x_k = ∂f_k/∂x_j. Let γ and γ' be piecewise-C^1 paths in a domain A from a to b, homotopic rel endpoints. Then ∫_γ ω = ∫_{γ'} ω.
(2) Proof. Reparametrize both paths on I = [α,β]. Translate the reverse path γ^o to I + (β−α). The concatenations γ∨γ^o and γ'∨γ^o are closed loops that are homotopic through loops. Theorem 1 (invariance of the integral of a closed form under deformation of circuits) then gives equal integrals; subtracting the common term gives the result.
(3) Definition 5. A domain is called 'contractile' if every loop deforms within A to a point. In modern terms this is simple connectedness. Star-shaped domains are examples.
(4) A form satisfying (1) is called 'fermée'. Theorem 2 (Cauchy): in a 'contractile' domain, the integral of a closed holomorphic form over any circuit is zero.
(5) Remark: for real variables, Theorem 1 extends to C^1 coefficients, with the aside 'est-ce que cela en vaut la peine ?'.
(6) Start of §3 on primitives. For g holomorphic, dg = Σ f_k dx_k is closed, and ∫_γ dg = g(γ(β)) − g(γ(α)). This leads to the standard result that a closed form on a simply connected domain has a primitive.

All of this is standard textbook material.
errors: Terminology: 'contractile' as defined (every loop deforms to a point) means simply connected, not contractible in the modern homotopy-theoretic sense. Nothing in the argument breaks, since only simple connectedness is used.

The proof implicitly relies on Theorem 1 being stated for free deformations of circuits through circuits. A homotopy of γ to γ' rel endpoints does give such a deformation of γ∨γ^o into γ'∨γ^o, so the argument is fine, if terse.
Minor: subtracting the integral over γ^o is left implicit; it relies on additivity of the integral under concatenation.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine typed lecture page on Cauchy's theorem for closed forms, unrelated to the motif material in the folder. It is most likely a reused sheet from course notes and contains nothing new.
transcription_corrections: 'γ_1(t)=γ_o(t-β+α)' should read γ_1(t) = γ^o(t − β + α), i.e. the opposite path γ^o, not γ_o.
At the bottom, 'définie dans I= ,' has a blank in the typescript; the intended reading is I = [α,β].
The last formula is cut off at the page edge: ... = g(γ(β)) − g(γ(α)).
'aussitôt' appears in the typescript as 'aussitôt' with a circumflex (typed 'aussitôt'); the text 'aussitôt le corollaire' is correct.
